fatal_errors: No controlled variation of multilayer modulation period or interface coherency is proposed.

The central mechanism is assigned to grain-boundary-mediated dislocation nucleation and twinning rather than semicoherent-interface blocking, stress localization, possible interfacial amorphization, and diffusion/interface slip.
The predicted strain hardening and twinning-induced plasticity do not reconstruct the creep-resistance maximum and stress-exponent minimum expected for the semicoherent multilayer.
The baseline is merely the undeformed state, not coherent-interface and grain-boundary-dominated multilayers tested under identical creep conditions.
Loading, temperature, time, coating thickness, indentation depth, and loading-rate boundaries are absent.
The cited studies concern different materials and predominantly 77 K tensile deformation, so they do not establish room-temperature nanoindentation-creep behavior in FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayers.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad setting of sustained deformation in an FCC/BCC HEA multilayer, but it does not identify the target governing variable: interface coherency controlled through layer thickness. It omits the key comparison among coherent, semicoherent, and grain-boundary-dominated architectures and instead advances a generic grain-boundary/dislocation/twinning hypothesis. Its proposed TEM experiment could detect those mechanisms, but without a controlled structural comparison it cannot distinguish the target hypothesis from ordinary load-induced defect accumulation. The falsification rule is also weak because absence of increased twinning would not test interface-controlled diffusion or slip. E2 supports grain-boundary dislocation and twin nucleation only in a different alloy at 77 K; E3 reports only a minor role for mechanically induced short-range order in another low-temperature alloy; and E1 concerns a γ/γ′ high-entropy superalloy model. Thus, the evidence does not validate the claimed creep mechanism or operating regime.
